sections.title: Definition of Big Data Ecosystem
sections.content: A Big Data Ecosystem is a collection of technologies, tools and processes used to collect, store, process and analyze large volumes of data. It helps organizations make better decisions using structured, semi-structured and unstructured data.

sections.title: Types of Data Generated
sections.content:
The bus transport system generates three types of data:
- Structured Data: Bus route maps, GPS coordinates and vehicle details.
- Semi-Structured Data: GPS logs, sensor records and XML/JSON files.
- Unstructured Data: CCTV videos, traffic images and audio recordings.

sections.title: Data Collection Sources
sections.content:
- Bus Route Maps: Provide route numbers, stops and distance information.
- Inductive Loop Detectors: Measure vehicle count and traffic density.
- CCTV Cameras: Capture traffic conditions, accidents and road congestion.
- GPS Updates: Provide real-time bus location, speed and arrival time.

sections.title: Big Data Processing Technologies
sections.content:
- Apache Kafka: Collects real-time sensor and GPS data.
- Hadoop HDFS: Stores large volumes of transport data.
- Apache Spark: Processes real-time and historical data.
- Hive: Performs data querying and analysis.
- Machine Learning: Predicts traffic congestion and bus delays.

sections.title: Big Data Lifecycle
sections.content:
- Data Generation: Data is generated from GPS, CCTV and sensors.
- Data Collection: Data is collected through ingestion tools.
- Data Storage: Data is stored in HDFS or cloud storage.
- Data Processing: Spark processes collected data.
- Data Analysis: Analytics identifies traffic patterns and delays.
- Data Visualization: Results are displayed using dashboards.

sections.title: Key Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
- Data Engineer: Collects and manages data pipelines.
- Data Scientist: Develops predictive models.
- Data Analyst: Identifies traffic patterns and delays.
- System Administrator: Maintains storage and infrastructure.
- Transport Manager: Uses analytical results for decision-making.

sections.title: Big Data Ecosystem Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
DATA SOURCES (GPS, CCTV, Sensors, Route Map) → DATA COLLECTION (Kafka) → DATA STORAGE (HDFS) → DATA PROCESSING (Spark) → DATA ANALYTICS (Machine Learning) → VISUALIZATION (Dashboard) → OPTIMIZED BUS TRANSPORT.

sections.title: Definition of Big Data
sections.content: Big Data refers to extremely large and complex datasets that cannot be efficiently processed using traditional data processing systems. It requires advanced technologies to store, manage and analyze data.

sections.title: Characteristics of Big Data (5 Vs)
sections.content:
- Volume: Huge amount of data generated.
- Velocity: Speed at which data is generated and processed.
- Variety: Different types of data.
- Veracity: Accuracy and reliability of data.
- Value: Useful information obtained from data.

sections.title: Convergence of Key Technologies
sections.content:
- Cloud Computing: Provides scalable storage and computing.
- Internet of Things (IoT): Generates continuous sensor data.
- Social Media: Produces large volumes of user-generated data.
- Artificial Intelligence: Supports intelligent data analysis.
- Distributed Computing: Processes data across multiple systems.

sections.title: Business Trends Contributing to Growth
sections.content:
- Digital Transformation: Businesses move towards digital platforms.
- E-Commerce: Generates customer and transaction data.
- Mobile Applications: Produce location and usage data.
- Personalization: Provides customer-specific recommendations.
- Real-Time Decision Making: Supports faster business decisions.

sections.title: Big Data Technologies and Tools
sections.content:
Technology — Purpose:
- Hadoop — Distributed storage and processing.
- Spark — Fast data processing.
- Kafka — Real-time data collection.
- Hive — Data querying.
- NoSQL — Flexible data storage.
- MongoDB — Document database.

sections.title: Real-Time Applications and Examples
sections.content:
- Healthcare: Disease prediction and patient monitoring.
- Banking: Fraud detection.
- Transportation: Traffic prediction.
- E-Commerce: Product recommendations.
- Social Media: Customer behaviour analysis.
- Weather Forecasting: Climate prediction.

sections.title: Big Data Characteristics Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
BIG DATA → Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value → BUSINESS INSIGHTS.

sections.title: Definition of Hadoop Ecosystem
sections.content: Hadoop Ecosystem is a collection of open-source tools and technologies used to store, process and analyze large datasets across distributed computer systems. It provides scalability, fault tolerance and distributed processing.

sections.title: Hadoop Core Components
sections.content:
- Hadoop Common: Provides common libraries and utilities.
- HDFS: Stores data across multiple machines.
- YARN: Manages cluster resources and job scheduling.
- MapReduce: Processes large datasets in parallel.

sections.title: Hadoop Distributed Storage
sections.content:
- HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) stores large files across multiple DataNodes.
- NameNode: Maintains file system metadata.
- DataNode: Stores actual data blocks.
- Block Replication: Creates multiple copies of data.
- Fault Tolerance: Recovers data when a node fails.

sections.title: Hadoop Data Processing
sections.content:
- MapReduce processes large datasets using two major functions:
- Mapper: Converts input data into intermediate key-value pairs.
- Reducer: Processes grouped values and generates final output.
- YARN allocates resources and manages execution.

sections.title: Hadoop Ecosystem Tools
sections.content:
Tool — Function:
- Pig — Data analysis using Pig Latin.
- Hive — SQL-like data querying.
- HBase — NoSQL database.
- Sqoop — Transfers data between RDBMS and Hadoop.
- Flume — Collects log data.
- Oozie — Workflow scheduling.
- ZooKeeper — Distributed coordination.

sections.title: Applications of Hadoop
sections.content:
- Banking: Fraud detection.
- Healthcare: Medical data analysis.
- E-Commerce: Customer behaviour analysis.
- Social Media: Large-scale data processing.
- Telecommunication: Network log analysis.
- Retail: Sales forecasting.

sections.title: Hadoop Ecosystem Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
DATA SOURCES → DATA INGESTION (Sqoop, Flume) → HDFS → YARN → MapReduce → HIVE/PIG/HBASE → DATA ANALYTICS → FINAL OUTPUT.

subtopics: Definition of Structured and Unstructured Data

sections.title: Definition of Structured and Unstructured Data
sections.content:
Structured Data: Data organized in a predefined format, usually rows and columns.
Unstructured Data: Data that does not follow a predefined tabular structure.
Examples: Database records, images, videos and documents.

sections.title: Characteristics of Structured Data
sections.content:
- Organized in rows and columns.
- Follows a predefined schema.
- Easy to search and query.
- Stored in relational databases.
- Supports SQL operations.
Examples: Student records, bank transactions and employee details.

sections.title: Characteristics of Unstructured Data
sections.content:
- Does not follow a fixed schema.
- Contains complex data formats.
- Difficult to process using traditional databases.
- Requires advanced processing tools.
- Stored in data lakes and distributed storage systems.
Examples: Images, videos, emails, audio and social media posts.

sections.title: Comparison Between Data Types
sections.content:
Structured Data vs Unstructured Data:
- Fixed schema vs No fixed schema.
- Rows and columns vs Different formats.
- Easy to query vs Complex to query.
- SQL databases vs NoSQL/Data Lakes.
- Highly organized vs Less organized.
- Example: Tables vs Videos.

sections.title: Crowdsourcing Analytics
sections.content:
Crowdsourcing Analytics is the process of collecting data, ideas and contributions from a large group of people through online platforms.
Working: Collect information from users; store the collected data; analyze user contributions; identify patterns and trends; generate useful insights.
Example: Customer reviews and online surveys.

sections.title: Inter-Firewall and Trans-Firewall Analytics
sections.content:
Inter-Firewall Analytics:
- Combines and analyzes data across organizational boundaries.
- Supports collaboration between different organizations.
- Example: Data sharing between banks and financial institutions.

Trans-Firewall Analytics:
- Uses data that crosses the organization's firewall, combining internal and external data.
- Helps organizations gain additional business insights.
- Example: Combining internal sales data with external market trends and social media data.

sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
BIG DATA → STRUCTURED DATA (Tables, Records, SQL) / SEMI-STRUCTURED DATA (JSON, XML, Logs) / UNSTRUCTURED DATA (Images, Videos, Audio) → DATA ANALYTICS.

questions.topic: NoSQL Distribution Models and CAP Theorem

sections.title: Definition of NoSQL Database
sections.content:
NoSQL (Not Only SQL) is a non-relational database used to store and manage large volumes of structured, semi-structured and unstructured data.
It provides flexible schema, horizontal scalability, high availability and distributed data storage.
Examples: MongoDB, Cassandra, HBase and Redis.

sections.title: NoSQL Distribution Models
sections.content:
NoSQL databases distribute data across multiple servers to improve performance and availability.
- Single Server: All data is stored on one server.
- Sharding: Data is divided and distributed across multiple servers.
- Replication: Multiple copies of data are maintained on different servers.
- Master-Slave: One master handles writes and slaves maintain copies.
- Master-Master: Multiple masters accept read and write operations.

sections.title: Master-Slave Replication
sections.content:
Master-Slave Replication is a distribution model in which one master server manages write operations and replicates data to one or more slave servers.
Working: Client sends a write request to the master; master updates its database; changes are replicated to slave servers; slaves handle read requests; if the master fails, a slave may be promoted through failover.
Advantages: Read scalability, data availability, backup support and reduced load on master.

sections.title: Master-Master Replication
sections.content:
Master-Master Replication is a model in which multiple database servers act as masters and accept read and write operations.
Working: Client sends requests to any master; each master updates its local database; changes are synchronized between masters; conflicting updates are resolved using conflict-resolution methods.
Advantages: High availability, write scalability and better distribution of workload.

sections.title: CAP Theorem
sections.content:
The CAP Theorem states that a distributed database system can guarantee at most two of the following three properties during a network partition:
- Consistency (C): Every read receives the latest successful write.
- Availability (A): Every request receives a response.
- Partition Tolerance (P): System continues operating despite network communication failures.

sections.title: Consistency and Availability Trade-offs
sections.content:
During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.
- CP System: Consistency + Partition Tolerance; may reject requests; maintains consistent data. Example: HBase (typical configuration).
- AP System: Availability + Partition Tolerance; continues responding; may return stale data. Example: Cassandra (tunable consistency).
- CA: Consistency and availability can be achieved when there is no network partition.

sections.title: NoSQL Distribution Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
CLIENT → MASTER SERVER → SLAVE 1 / SLAVE 2 (read requests); MASTER receives write requests.
CAP: CONSISTENCY / AVAILABILITY / PARTITION TOLERANCE.

questions.topic: Cassandra Data Model and CRUD Operations

sections.title: Definition of Apache Cassandra
sections.content:
Apache Cassandra is an open-source, distributed NoSQL database designed to handle large amounts of data across multiple servers.
Features: High availability, fault tolerance, horizontal scalability and peer-to-peer architecture.

sections.title: Cassandra Data Model
sections.content:
Cassandra uses a wide-column data model to store data.
- Keyspace: Logical container for tables.
- Table: Stores data in rows and columns.
- Partition Key: Determines the node where data is stored.
- Clustering Column: Determines the order of rows within a partition.
- Column: Stores individual data values.

sections.title: Keyspace and Table Structure
CRUD Operations
sections.content:
CRUD represents four basic database operations.
CREATE – Insert Data:
```sql
INSERT INTO students (roll_no, name, department, grade) VALUES (101, 'Raja', 'AI&DS', 'A');
```
READ – Retrieve Data:
```sql
SELECT * FROM students;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE roll_no = 101;
```
UPDATE – Modify Data:
```sql
UPDATE students SET grade = 'A+' WHERE roll_no = 101;
```
DELETE – Remove Data:
```sql
DELETE FROM students WHERE roll_no = 101;
```

sections.title: CQL Commands and Syntax
sections.content:
CQL (Cassandra Query Language) is used to communicate with Cassandra databases.
- CREATE KEYSPACE: Creates a keyspace.
- CREATE TABLE: Creates a table.
- INSERT: Inserts records.
- SELECT: Retrieves records.
- UPDATE: Modifies records.
- DELETE: Removes records.
- DROP TABLE: Deletes a table.

sections.title: Cassandra Data Retrieval and Examples
sections.content:
Example student table:
roll_no | name | department | grade
101 | Raja | AI&DS | A
102 | Kumar | CSE | B
103 | Arun | AI&DS | A+
Retrieve AI&DS students (the supplied example query):
```sql
SELECT * FROM students WHERE roll_no = 101;
```
Cassandra efficiently retrieves records using partition keys. Cassandra requires suitable primary-key-based queries. Filtering on non-key columns may require additional configuration or indexing.

sections.title: Cassandra Data Model Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
CASSANDRA → KEYSPACE → TABLE → PARTITION KEY / COLUMNS → PARTITION → ROWS → DATA VALUES.

sections.title: Definition of MongoDB
sections.content:
MongoDB is an open-source, document-oriented NoSQL database that stores data in flexible BSON (Binary JSON) documents.
Features: Flexible schema, document-based storage, horizontal scalability, high availability and fast data retrieval.

sections.title: MongoDB Database and Collection
sections.content:
MongoDB stores data using the following hierarchy:
- Database: Container for collections.
- Collection: Group of related documents.
- Document: Individual record stored in BSON format.
- Field: Individual data item.
Select database:
```javascript
use college
```
Create or select collection:
```javascript
db.createCollection("students")
```

sections.title: Insert Operations
sections.content:
The insertOne() method inserts one student record.
```javascript
db.students.insertOne({roll_no: 115, name: "Raja", grade: "Fifth", hobbies: "Basketball", DOJ: "2026-06-10"})
```
Purpose: Adds a new document to the collection.

sections.title: Read and Retrieve Operations
sections.content:
The find() method retrieves documents.
```javascript
db.students.find({roll_no: 115})
```
Retrieve all student records:
```javascript
db.students.find()
```

sections.title: Update Operations
sections.content:
The updateOne() method modifies an existing document.
```javascript
db.students.updateOne({name: "Raja"}, {$set: {hobbies: "Football"}})
```
Purpose: $set updates the specified field without replacing the entire document.

sections.title: Delete and Filtering Operations
sections.content:
Delete fifth-grade students:
```javascript
db.students.deleteMany({grade: "Fifth"})
```
Retrieve students whose names start with V:
```javascript
db.students.find({name: {$regex: "^V", $options: "i"}})
```
- $regex: Performs pattern matching.
- ^V: Matches names starting with V.
- i: Ignores uppercase and lowercase differences.

sections.title: MongoDB CRUD Operation Flow Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
MONGODB → DATABASE → COLLECTION → CREATE/INSERT; READ/FIND; UPDATE/MODIFY; DELETE/REMOVE → DOCUMENTS.

questions.topic: NoSQL Aggregate and Graph Data Models
subtopics: Advantages and Applications of Data Models

sections.title: Definition of NoSQL Data Models
sections.content:
NoSQL is a non-relational database approach designed to store and manage large volumes of distributed and flexible data.
Major types: Key-Value Model, Document Model, Column-Family Model and Graph Model.

sections.title: Aggregate Data Models
sections.content:
An Aggregate Data Model groups related data into a single logical unit called an aggregate.
Features: Stores related information together; supports efficient data retrieval; reduces complex joins; suitable for distributed databases.
Example: A customer record containing customer details, address and order information.

sections.title: Key-Value Data Model
sections.content:
A Key-Value Model stores data as a collection of unique keys and their corresponding values.
Features: Simple data structure, fast data retrieval, unique keys and flexible values.
Example: 101 → Raja; 102 → Kumar; 103 → Arun. Database: Redis.

sections.title: Document Data Model
sections.content:
A Document Data Model stores data in documents, usually in JSON, BSON or XML format.
Features: Flexible schema, nested data support, easy data modification and support for complex documents.
Example:
```json
{"roll_no":101,"name":"Raja","department":"AI&DS","hobbies":["Cricket","Music"]}
```
Database: MongoDB.

sections.title: Graph Data Model
sections.content:
A Graph Data Model represents data using nodes, edges and properties.
- Nodes: Represent entities.
- Edges: Represent relationships.
- Properties: Store additional information.
Example: Student node; College node; Studies at edge. Database: Neo4j.

sections.title: Advantages and Applications of Data Models
sections.content:
Model — Advantages — Applications:
- Key-Value — Fast access — Caching.
- Document — Flexible schema — Content management.
- Column-Family — Distributed storage — Big Data.
- Graph — Relationship analysis — Social networks.
- Aggregate — Efficient data grouping — E-Commerce.

sections.title: NoSQL Data Models Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
NoSQL → Key-Value (Redis), Document (MongoDB), Column-Family (Cassandra), Graph (Neo4j).

sections.title: Definition of MapReduce
sections.content:
MapReduce is a distributed programming model used to process large datasets across multiple computers in a Hadoop cluster.
- Mapper: Converts input data into intermediate key-value pairs.
- Reducer: Processes grouped values and generates final output.

sections.title: Grocery Dataset and Input Records
sections.content:
Consider the following transactions:
ID 1: Paneer, Bread, Eggs, Milk
ID 2: Eggs, Paneer, Bread
ID 3: Milk, Bread, Eggs
ID 4: Milk, Paneer
ID 5: Bread, Eggs
Objective: Calculate the total number of times each item is purchased.

sections.title: Mapper Function
sections.content:
The Mapper reads each transaction and generates a key-value pair. Key = Item name; Value = 1.
Example input: Paneer, Bread, Eggs, Milk
Output: (Paneer, 1), (Bread, 1), (Eggs, 1), (Milk, 1).

sections.title: Intermediate Key-Value Pairs
sections.content:
Intermediate pairs:
(Paneer,1), (Bread,1), (Eggs,1), (Milk,1)
(Eggs,1), (Paneer,1), (Bread,1)
(Milk,1), (Bread,1), (Eggs,1)
(Milk,1), (Paneer,1)
(Bread,1), (Eggs,1)

sections.title: Shuffle and Sort Process
sections.content:
Shuffle and Sort groups all values having the same key.
Paneer → [1,1,1]
Bread → [1,1,1,1]
Eggs → [1,1,1,1]
Milk → [1,1,1]
It transfers and groups Mapper outputs before Reducer execution.

sections.title: Reducer Function and Final Output
sections.content:
Reducer adds all values associated with each key.
```text
Reduce(key, values):
    total = SUM(values)
    Output(key, total)
```
Final output: Paneer 3; Bread 4; Eggs 4; Milk 3.
Result: Bread and Eggs are the most frequently purchased items.

sections.title: MapReduce Workflow Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
INPUT DATASET → INPUT SPLIT → MAPPER → KEY-VALUE PAIRS (Item,1) → SHUFFLE & SORT → REDUCER (SUM) → FINAL OUTPUT.

sections.title: Definition of YARN
sections.content:
YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator) is the resource management and job scheduling framework of Hadoop. It manages cluster resources and allocates them to different applications.
Functions: Resource allocation, job scheduling, application management and cluster resource monitoring.

sections.title: YARN Architecture Components
sections.content: YARN consists of four major components: ResourceManager, NodeManager, ApplicationMaster and Container. These components work together to execute applications across a Hadoop cluster.

sections.title: ResourceManager
sections.content:
ResourceManager (RM) is the master component responsible for managing resources across the cluster.
Functions: Allocates cluster resources; schedules application requests; monitors resource availability; coordinates with NodeManagers.
It contains Scheduler (allocates resources based on scheduling policies) and ApplicationsManager (accepts application submissions and manages ApplicationMaster startup).

sections.title: NodeManager
sections.content:
NodeManager (NM) is responsible for managing individual worker nodes.
Functions: Monitors node resources; manages containers; reports node status to ResourceManager; monitors container execution.
Each worker node runs one NodeManager.

sections.title: ApplicationMaster and Containers
sections.content:
ApplicationMaster (AM): Manages a particular application; requests resources from ResourceManager; coordinates task execution; monitors application progress.
Container: A unit of allocated resources; provides CPU and memory for executing tasks; runs application processes on worker nodes.

sections.title: YARN Job Execution and Scheduling
sections.content:
Steps: Client submits an application to ResourceManager; ResourceManager allocates a container to start ApplicationMaster; ApplicationMaster registers with ResourceManager; ApplicationMaster requests additional containers; ResourceManager allocates resources; NodeManagers launch tasks inside containers; ApplicationMaster monitors execution and reports completion.
Example: For a MapReduce job, YARN allocates containers to execute Mapper and Reducer tasks across worker nodes.

sections.title: YARN Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
CLIENT → RESOURCE MANAGER → APPLICATION MASTER → RESOURCE REQUEST → NODE MANAGERS → CONTAINERS → TASKS → JOB COMPLETION.

sections.title: Definition of MapReduce Job Execution
sections.content: MapReduce Job Execution is the process of executing a distributed data processing task using Mapper and Reducer functions in a Hadoop cluster. It converts input data into intermediate key-value pairs and produces final output.

sections.title: Job Submission Process
sections.content:
- Client submits a MapReduce job to Hadoop.
- Job configuration and JAR files are submitted.
- Input and output paths are specified.
- Hadoop validates the job configuration.
- The job is submitted to the cluster for execution.

sections.title: Input Splitting and Record Reading
sections.content:
- InputFormat: Divides input files into logical input splits.
- InputSplit: Represents a portion of input data.
- RecordReader: Converts input data into key-value records.
- Each split is processed by a separate Mapper task.

sections.title: Mapper and Combiner Execution
sections.content:
Mapper reads input key-value pairs, processes individual records and generates intermediate key-value pairs.
Combiner performs local aggregation of Mapper output, reduces the amount of data transferred and minimizes network communication.
Example: (A,1),(A,1),(B,1),(A,1) → (A,3),(B,1).

sections.title: Shuffle and Sort Process
sections.content:
- Partitioning: Divides Mapper output among Reducers.
- Shuffling: Transfers intermediate data to Reducers.
- Sorting: Groups records based on keys.
- Grouping: Combines values belonging to the same key.
Example: (A,1),(A,1),(A,1),(B,1) → (A,[1,1,1]), (B,[1]).

sections.title: Reducer Execution and Output Storage
sections.content:
Reducer receives grouped key-value pairs; processes each key and its associated values; performs aggregation or computation; generates final output; OutputFormat writes results into HDFS.
Example: Word count produces the total occurrence of each word.
Classic MapReduce vs YARN:
- Classic: JobTracker and TaskTracker; JobTracker manages resources and jobs; limited scalability; primarily MapReduce.
- YARN: ResourceManager and NodeManager; resource and application management are separated; better scalability; supports multiple processing frameworks.

sections.title: MapReduce Job Execution Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
JOB SUBMISSION → INPUT FORMAT → INPUT SPLITS → RECORD READER → MAPPER → COMBINER → SHUFFLE & SORT → REDUCER → OUTPUT FORMAT → HDFS.

subtopics: Definition of MapReduce Types and Formats

sections.title: Definition of MapReduce Types and Formats
sections.content: MapReduce is a distributed processing model that uses Mapper and Reducer functions to process large datasets. InputFormat and OutputFormat define how input data is read and how processed results are written.

sections.title: Types of MapReduce Applications
sections.content:
- Map-only Job: Performs processing using only the Mapper without a Reducer.
- Map-Reduce Job: Uses both Mapper and Reducer for processing.
- Chained MapReduce Job: Executes multiple MapReduce jobs sequentially.
Examples: Map-only—data filtering; Map-Reduce—word counting; chained jobs—multi-stage data analysis.

sections.title: InputFormat and Its Types
sections.content:
InputFormat defines how input files are divided into input splits and read by Mapper tasks.
- TextInputFormat: Reads text files line by line.
- KeyValueTextInputFormat: Reads key-value text records.
- SequenceFileInputFormat: Reads binary sequence files.
- NLineInputFormat: Creates splits based on number of lines.
- CombineFileInputFormat: Combines multiple small files.

sections.title: OutputFormat and Its Types
sections.content:
OutputFormat defines how Reducer output is written to storage.
- TextOutputFormat: Writes output as text.
- SequenceFileOutputFormat: Writes binary sequence files.
- MapFileOutputFormat: Writes MapFile format.
- NullOutputFormat: Produces no output file.
- DBOutputFormat: Writes output to a database.

sections.title: MapReduce Task Execution
sections.content: Steps: Input files are divided into splits; Mapper reads input records; Mapper generates intermediate key-value pairs; Combiner performs local aggregation if configured; Shuffle and Sort group intermediate data; Reducer processes grouped records; OutputFormat writes final results.

sections.title: Failures in MapReduce and YARN
sections.content:
Common failures and handling:
- Mapper Failure: Re-execute failed task.
- Reducer Failure: Re-execute failed task.
- Node Failure: Reschedule tasks on another node.
- ApplicationMaster Failure: Restart ApplicationMaster if configured.
- ResourceManager Failure: ResourceManager recovery and failover.
- Network Failure: Retry communication and recover tasks.
Fault-tolerance techniques: Task re-execution, HDFS replication, heartbeat monitoring, speculative execution, ResourceManager high availability and application recovery.

sections.title: MapReduce Input-Output Flow Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
INPUT FILES → INPUT FORMAT → INPUT SPLITS → MAPPER → INTERMEDIATE DATA → SHUFFLE & SORT → REDUCER → OUTPUT FORMAT → OUTPUT FILES.

sections.title: Definition of HDFS
sections.content:
HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) is a distributed file system used to store large datasets across multiple computers in a Hadoop cluster.
Features: Distributed storage, fault tolerance, high throughput, scalability and data replication.

sections.title: HDFS Architecture Components
sections.content:
Major components:
- NameNode: Maintains file system metadata.
- DataNode: Stores actual data blocks.
- Secondary NameNode: Periodically merges file system image and edit logs to create checkpoints.
- Client: Communicates with NameNode and DataNodes to access files.

sections.title: NameNode and DataNode
sections.content:
NameNode: Acts as the master node; maintains file and directory information; stores block locations; manages file permissions; monitors DataNodes using heartbeats.
DataNode: Acts as a worker node; stores actual data blocks; performs read and write operations; sends block reports to NameNode; maintains replicated blocks.
Secondary NameNode: Performs checkpointing; merges FsImage and EditLog; helps reduce metadata recovery work.

sections.title: HDFS Block Management and Replication
sections.content:
HDFS divides large files into fixed-size blocks.
- Block: A part of a large file.
- Replication: Creates multiple copies of blocks.
- Block Placement: Distributes replicas across DataNodes.
- Fault Tolerance: Allows data recovery when a DataNode fails.
Example: A file divided into three blocks is stored across different DataNodes with multiple replicas.

sections.title: HDFS Read and Write Operations
sections.content:
Read Operation: Client requests a file from NameNode; NameNode provides block locations; client connects to the nearest suitable DataNode; DataNode sends required blocks; client combines blocks to reconstruct the file.
Write Operation: Client requests file creation; NameNode checks permissions and selects DataNodes; client divides data into blocks; blocks are written through a DataNode replication pipeline; acknowledgements are returned to the client.

sections.title: HDFS Commands and File Operations
sections.content:
HDFS commands:
```bash
hdfs dfs -ls /
hdfs dfs -mkdir /sample
hdfs dfs -put file.txt /sample/
hdfs dfs -cat /sample/file.txt
```
Alternative upload: `hdfs dfs -copyFromLocal file.txt /sample/`.
Additional commands: `hdfs dfs -get /sample/file.txt .` downloads a file; `hdfs dfs -rm /sample/file.txt` deletes a file.

sections.title: HDFS Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
CLIENT → NAMENODE (Metadata Manager) → DATANODE 1 / DATANODE 2 (data blocks); SECONDARY NAMENODE performs checkpointing.

sections.title: Definition of Spark Streaming
sections.content:
Apache Spark Streaming is a component of Apache Spark used to process continuous streams of real-time data.
It supports real-time data processing, stream analysis, fault tolerance and integration with Kafka.

sections.title: IoT Sensor Data Collection and HDFS Storage
sections.content:
IoT sensors installed in machines collect temperature, vibration, pressure, speed, humidity and machine operating time.
Storage process: Sensors generate continuous data; data is collected through IoT gateways; data is transferred to the storage system; HDFS stores collected data in distributed blocks; historical data is used for machine learning analysis.

sections.title: Kafka Architecture and Data Streaming
sections.content:
Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform used to collect and transfer real-time sensor data.
- Producer: Sends sensor data to Kafka.
- Topic: Stores categorized events.
- Broker: Manages messages.
- Consumer: Reads messages from topics.
- Partition: Divides topic data for parallel processing.
Working: IoT sensors send data through producers; Kafka stores messages in topics; Spark consumes messages; real-time data is processed for analysis.

sections.title: Real-Time Data Processing Using PySpark
sections.content:
PySpark is the Python API for Apache Spark.
The supplied example reads a Kafka topic as a stream and prints message values:
```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("IoTMonitoring").getOrCreate()
df = spark.readStream.format("kafka").option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092").option("subscribe", "machine_data").load()
data = df.selectExpr("CAST(value AS STRING)")
query = data.writeStream.format("console").start()
query.awaitTermination()
```
Processing steps: Connect Spark to Kafka; read sensor messages; parse JSON records; filter invalid values; calculate statistics; identify abnormal conditions; store processed results in HDFS.

sections.title: Python-Based Machine Learning Integration
sections.content:
Machine learning models predict machine failures using historical and real-time sensor data.
Steps: Collect historical sensor data from HDFS; preprocess and clean; train a Python ML model; evaluate with test data; load the trained model into Spark; predict failures using incoming sensor values.
Example algorithms: Random Forest, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machine.
Example prediction: Temperature = 95°C; Vibration = High; Failure Risk = HIGH.

sections.title: Real-Time Failure Prediction and Applications
sections.content:
Working: Spark continuously processes sensor data; machine learning identifies abnormal patterns; failure probability is calculated; alerts are generated when abnormal conditions occur; maintenance teams receive notifications.
Advantages: Reduces machine downtime; improves production efficiency; prevents unexpected failures; reduces maintenance costs; improves equipment lifetime.

sections.title: Spark Streaming Predictive Maintenance Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
IoT MACHINE SENSORS → DATA COLLECTION → KAFKA → SPARK STREAMING → PYSPARK → HDFS / ML MODEL → FAILURE DETECTION → ALERT GENERATION → PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE.

sections.title: Definition of Avro
sections.content:
Apache Avro is a data serialization framework used to exchange and store data in a compact binary format. It is commonly used in Hadoop environments for efficient data serialization.
Features: Schema-based serialization, compact binary format, language-independent, supports data exchange and schema evolution.

sections.title: Avro Data Serialization
sections.content:
Data Serialization is the process of converting data objects into a format suitable for storage or transmission.
Avro supports Binary Format (compact binary representation) and JSON Format (readable JSON representation of schemas and data).
Advantages: Reduces storage requirements; improves data transfer efficiency; supports multiple programming languages; enables efficient data exchange.

sections.title: Avro Schema and Data Types
sections.content:
Avro uses a schema to define the structure of data.
Example:
```json
{"type":"record","name":"Student","fields":[{"name":"roll_no","type":"int"},{"name":"name","type":"string"},{"name":"department","type":"string"}]}
```
Types: null, boolean, int, long, float, double, string, bytes, record, array, map and enum.

sections.title: Cassandra Data Storage and Processing
sections.content:
Apache Cassandra stores large amounts of distributed data using a wide-column data model.
Features: Distributed architecture, peer-to-peer communication, high availability, replication and horizontal scalability.
Cassandra stores operational data and supports fast read and write operations.

sections.title: Cassandra-Hadoop Integration Process
sections.content:
Cassandra integrates with Hadoop to combine distributed storage and large-scale data processing.
Steps: Data is stored in Cassandra tables; Hadoop connects through Cassandra-Hadoop integration interfaces; Cassandra data is accessed by Hadoop MapReduce jobs; Mapper reads records; Reducer processes and aggregates data; results are stored in HDFS or Cassandra.

sections.title: Big Data Analytics Using Cassandra and Hadoop
sections.content:
Example: E-Commerce Data Analysis. Cassandra stores customer transactions; Hadoop reads transaction records; MapReduce analyzes purchase patterns; Reducer calculates total sales; results are stored in HDFS; Hive can query processed results.
Advantages: Large-scale data processing, flexible distributed storage, high availability, efficient analytics and improved scalability.

sections.title: Cassandra-Hadoop Integration Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
DATA SOURCES → CASSANDRA (Data Storage) → HADOOP CONNECTOR → MAPREDUCE (Mapper → Reducer) → HDFS → DATA ANALYTICS → FINAL OUTPUT.

sections.title: Definition of Hadoop Streaming and Pipes
sections.content:
Hadoop Streaming is a Hadoop utility that allows users to create MapReduce applications using executable programs written in languages such as Python, Ruby and Perl.
Hadoop Pipes is a C++ API that allows developers to write Hadoop MapReduce applications using C++.
Both support MapReduce application development beyond Java.

sections.title: Hadoop Streaming Architecture
sections.content:
Hadoop Streaming uses standard input and standard output to communicate with Mapper and Reducer programs.
Components: Input Data in HDFS; Mapper Script; Reducer Script; Standard Input; Standard Output; Hadoop Framework manages task execution.

sections.title: Hadoop Streaming Working Process
sections.content: Steps: Input data is stored in HDFS; Hadoop divides data into input splits; Mapper executable receives records through standard input; Mapper generates intermediate key-value pairs through standard output; Hadoop performs shuffle and sort; Reducer receives grouped records; final output is stored in HDFS.

sections.title: Mapper and Reducer Implementation
sections.content:
Mapper and Reducer can be written in different scripting languages. Input is received through standard input; output is generated through standard output; key-value pairs are separated using delimiters, commonly tab characters.
Example input: Big Data Big Data. Mapper output: (Big,1), (Data,1), (Big,1), (Data,1). Reducer output: (Big,2), (Data,2).
Original Mapper and Reducer scripts are included in the programs array.

sections.title: Hadoop Pipes Architecture and Working
sections.content:
Hadoop Pipes provides a C++ API for writing Mapper and Reducer programs.
Working: Developer writes C++ Mapper and Reducer classes; C++ program communicates with Hadoop using the Pipes interface; Hadoop launches the application on worker nodes; Mapper processes input records; Reducer processes grouped key-value pairs; final results are stored in HDFS.
Features: C++ application development, distributed processing, communication between Hadoop and C++ programs and use of Hadoop MapReduce framework.

sections.title: Applications and Advantages
sections.content:
Applications: Log file analysis, word counting, large-scale text processing, data filtering and scientific data analysis.
Advantages: Supports multiple programming languages; reuses existing code; simplifies MapReduce development; supports distributed processing; reduces dependence on Java programming.

sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
INPUT DATA / HDFS → HADOOP STREAMING (Python/scripts) OR HADOOP PIPES (C++) → MAPPER → REDUCER → FINAL OUTPUT / HDFS.

sections.title: Definition of HBase
sections.content:
Apache HBase is an open-source, distributed, column-family NoSQL database built on top of HDFS. It is used to store and retrieve large amounts of sparse data in real time.
Features: Distributed storage, horizontal scalability, fault tolerance, random read and write access and strong consistency at row level.

sections.title: HBase Architecture Components
sections.content:
Important components:
- HMaster: Manages the HBase cluster and assigns regions.
- RegionServer: Handles read and write requests.
- ZooKeeper: Coordinates distributed services.
- HDFS: Provides distributed data storage.
- Region: A portion of an HBase table.
- WAL: Write-Ahead Log used for recovery.

sections.title: HBase Data Model and Storage
sections.content:
HBase uses a column-family data model.
- Table: Collection of rows.
- Row Key: Unique identifier for each row.
- Column Family: Group of related columns.
- Column Qualifier: Identifies an individual column.
- Cell: Stores a value with a timestamp.
- Timestamp: Maintains different versions of data.
Example: row 101, name Raja, department AI&DS; row 102, name Kumar, department CSE.

sections.title: HBase Operations and Working
sections.content:
Operations: create, put, get, scan, delete and disable.
Example commands:
```text
create 'students', 'details'
put 'students', '101', 'details:name', 'Raja'
get 'students', '101'
scan 'students'
delete 'students', '101', 'details:name'
```
Working: Client sends request; ZooKeeper helps locate RegionServer; RegionServer processes request; data is accessed through MemStore or BlockCache; data is stored persistently in HFiles on HDFS.

sections.title: HBase vs Traditional Relational Database
sections.content:
HBase vs Relational Database:
- HBase: NoSQL; column-family model; flexible columns; distributed storage; handles massive sparse data; horizontal scalability; no traditional SQL joins.
- Relational Database: SQL database; relational tables; fixed schema; commonly centralized or distributed; suitable for structured data; often uses vertical scaling; supports SQL joins.

sections.title: HBase Integration with MapReduce
sections.content:
Steps: HBase stores large datasets; MapReduce connects to HBase tables; Mapper reads records from HBase; Mapper generates intermediate key-value pairs; Reducer processes and aggregates data; results are written to HBase or HDFS.
Applications: Customer behaviour analysis, log processing, financial data analysis and large-scale reporting.

sections.title: HBase Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
CLIENT → ZOOKEEPER → HMASTER (Region Assignment) → REGIONSERVERS → MEMSTORE / HFILES → HDFS.

subtopics: Hive Data Storage and File Formats

sections.title: Definition of Apache Hive
sections.content:
Apache Hive is a data warehouse infrastructure built on Hadoop that is used to query, manage and analyze large datasets. It provides an SQL-like language called Hive Query Language (HQL).
Features: SQL-like querying, distributed data processing, data warehousing, large-scale data analysis and integration with Hadoop.

sections.title: Hive Architecture Components
sections.content:
Major components:
- User Interface: Accepts user queries.
- Driver: Manages query execution.
- Compiler: Converts HQL into an execution plan.
- Optimizer: Optimizes the execution plan.
- Execution Engine: Executes the processing tasks.
- Metastore: Stores metadata.
- HDFS: Stores actual data.

sections.title: Hive Metastore and Query Processor
sections.content:
Metastore: Stores table information; maintains column names and data types; stores partition details; maintains database and schema information; usually uses a relational database to store metadata.
Query Processor: Receives HQL queries; parses and checks queries; generates execution plans; optimizes queries; sends tasks to the execution engine.

sections.title: Hive Query Execution Process
Hive Data Storage and File Formats
sections.content:
Hive stores data in HDFS.
- TextFile: Plain text storage.
- SequenceFile: Binary key-value format.
- ORC: Optimized columnar format.
- Parquet: Columnar storage format.
- Avro: Schema-based serialization.
Partitioning divides table data based on partition columns. Bucketing divides data into fixed groups using hash functions.

sections.title: Applications and Advantages of Hive
sections.content:
Applications: Data warehousing, log analysis, business intelligence, customer data analysis and report generation.
Advantages: Easy SQL-like queries, handles large datasets, integrates with Hadoop, supports multiple file formats and provides scalable data analysis.

sections.title: Hive Architecture Diagram
sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
USER/CLIENT → HIVE UI → DRIVER → COMPILER → OPTIMIZER → METASTORE / EXECUTION ENGINE → MAPREDUCE OR TEZ → HDFS → FINAL RESULT.

sections.title: Definition of Apache Spark
sections.content:
Apache Spark is an open-source, distributed computing framework used for fast processing and analysis of large datasets. It supports batch processing, real-time streaming, machine learning and graph processing.
Features: In-memory computing, fast data processing, fault tolerance, distributed computing and multiple language support.

sections.title: Spark Stack Architecture
sections.content: The Spark stack consists of different components that support distributed data processing. Important layers: Spark Core, Spark SQL, Spark Streaming, MLlib and GraphX. These components work on top of Spark Core.

sections.title: Spark Core
sections.content:
Spark Core is the foundation of the Apache Spark framework.
Functions: Task scheduling, memory management, distributed execution, fault recovery and RDD management.
RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset): A fault-tolerant collection of data distributed across multiple nodes.

sections.title: Spark SQL and Structured Data Processing
sections.content:
Spark SQL is used to process structured and semi-structured data.
Features: SQL query processing, DataFrame support, Dataset support, structured data analysis and integration with Hive.
Example:
```python
df = spark.read.csv("students.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
df.show()
```

sections.title: Spark Streaming and MLlib
sections.content:
Spark Streaming: Processes continuous data streams; supports real-time analytics; integrates with Kafka; processes sensor and log data.
MLlib: Provides machine learning algorithms; supports classification, regression, clustering and model evaluation.

sections.title: GraphX and Spark Applications
sections.content:
GraphX is a Spark component used for graph processing and analysis.
Functions: Graph construction, graph computation, relationship analysis and graph algorithms.
Applications of Spark: Fraud detection, recommendation systems, real-time monitoring, social network analysis, machine learning and Big Data analytics.

sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
SPARK STACK: SPARK SQL / STREAMING / MLLIB / GRAPHX → SPARK CORE → CLUSTER MANAGER → DISTRIBUTED STORAGE (HDFS).

sections.title: Definition of Hive and Pig
sections.content: Apache Hive is a Hadoop-based data warehouse tool used to query and analyze large datasets using HQL. Apache Pig is a high-level data processing platform that uses a scripting language called Pig Latin to process large datasets. Both simplify Big Data processing.

sections.title: Hive Data Types
sections.content:
Hive supports two major categories of data types.
Primitive: TINYINT (small integer), INT (integer), BIGINT (large integer), FLOAT, DOUBLE, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE and TIMESTAMP.
Complex: ARRAY (collection of values), MAP (key-value pairs), STRUCT (group of named fields) and UNIONTYPE (one value from multiple permitted types).

sections.title: Hive File Formats
sections.content:
Hive supports different file formats:
- TextFile: Plain text.
- SequenceFile: Binary key-value.
- ORC: Optimized columnar.
- Parquet: Columnar storage.
- Avro: Schema-based format.
Advantages of columnar formats: Better compression, faster analytical queries, reduced disk I/O and efficient data scanning.

sections.title: Hive Query Language (HQL)
HQL Data Manipulation Operations
sections.content:
Data Manipulation Language (DML) is used to manage records in Hive tables.
LOAD DATA:
```sql
LOAD DATA LOCAL INPATH '/home/students.csv' INTO TABLE students;
```
INSERT:
```sql
INSERT INTO TABLE students VALUES (102, 'Kumar', 'CSE');
```
SELECT:
```sql
SELECT * FROM students;
```
UPDATE:
```sql
UPDATE students SET department = 'AI&DS' WHERE roll_no = 101;
```
DELETE:
```sql
DELETE FROM students WHERE roll_no = 102;
```
Note: Hive UPDATE and DELETE require suitable transactional table configuration, commonly ACID/transactional ORC tables.

sections.title: HBase and Pig Data Models – Comparison
sections.content:
HBase Data Model: Stores data in tables; uses row keys; groups columns into column families; supports multiple column qualifiers; stores timestamped cell values.
Pig Data Model: Atom (single value), Tuple (ordered collection of fields), Bag (collection of tuples), Map (key-value pairs) and Relation (collection of tuples).
Comparison: HBase is a column-family database for persistent data, using row keys and column families. Pig is a data processing model for datasets, using tuples and bags.

sections.content:
Exam-friendly block diagram:
BIG DATA TOOLS → HIVE (HQL QUERIES → DATA ANALYSIS) / PIG (PIG LATIN → DATA PROCESSING) → HADOOP/HDFS.
Pig model: ATOM, TUPLE, BAG, MAP.
